text: The black market is where a defeated country prices what is left of itself: food, space, protection, and the men who enforce all three. Shozo Hirono and the friends he came home with go to work inside that economy, where the war they survived has been replaced by a smaller one with the same appetite and no fixed front. Kinji Fukasaku filmed this in 1973, far enough from the occupation years to treat the inherited language of loyalty and obligation as a collections business with better manners. Ninety-nine minutes, and nearly all of them go to men rearranging who owes what to whom, in alliances that hold until the next payment comes due. Kinema Junpo's all-time list of Japanese films carries it, and a Baeksang went to it as best film.

Paper is what Jihei manufactures, and paper is what every obligation in his life is written on. He is prosperous, married, a father, and entirely fluent in what eighteenth-century Japan permits a man of his standing; the fluency stops helping him the day he meets the courtesan Koharu. Masahiro Shinoda takes 105 minutes and lets desire behave exactly like debt, borrowed against the household, the business and the family name, compounding while the sensible parties advise restraint. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of its year. The rules are never hidden from Jihei; they are recited to him constantly, by relatives, by custom, by his own good sense, and the reciting changes nothing, which is the part that stings.

An engineer arrives from Tokyo with a job that sounds small: sink a well so a sugar mill can run. What the well requires turns out to be the island itself, its ground and its labor and its weather, and the Futori clan, who hold all of that and have never needed a mill. Japan sent the film to the Academy Awards; Kinema Junpo called it the best of 1968 and has kept it on the all-time list since. Shōhei Imamura takes 173 minutes over the transaction, long enough for tides, heat and kinship rules to set the pace instead of the plot. The stakes are not whether the well gets drilled. They are what a place surrenders when it agrees to be useful to somewhere else, and whether the agreement was ever offered as a choice.

The household is ranked: a father who earns, a mother who maintains, one son whose exam results are acceptable and one whose are not. The remedy is procurement, a private tutor hired to raise the underperforming member, and Yoshimitsu Morita treats the whole arrangement less as a family than as a small firm with a performance problem. What makes the comedy uncomfortable is that everyone consents to it. Affection is issued through seating, grades and portions; the tutor has access to all three, and the house has no procedure for an outsider who takes the job seriously. Kinema Junpo gave it the year's best film. 107 minutes, and the target is never the boy who fails, it is the certainty that failing is the only thing wrong here.

Friendship is the whole of the plot, and the film carries no anxiety about that. Two boys meet where the river runs out into Osaka's harbor, and because their parents make a living off that water, the world the boys share is a working one, with hours, weather and other people's business running through it, and no clean line between play and labor. Kōhei Oguri keeps to 105 minutes and to what children are allowed to see, which is rarely the same as what they are told. Kinema Junpo made it the best film of 1981, and Japan sent it to the Academy Awards as its international feature. What stands to be lost is not safety but ignorance: the hour a child learns what the adults have been managing, and cannot go back to not knowing it.

1926 was recent history in 1960, close enough that the first audiences could have furnished the rooms from memory. Kon Ichikawa keeps the scale domestic, a household of a few people, a sister and a brother, and the arrangement between them that the rest of the house quietly rests on. 98 minutes, filed as drama and comedy, which is accurate in the way families are both at once: the relative who is unbearable at the table is also the joke everyone shares afterward. Nothing dramatic has to occur for the stakes to show, since a household of this kind runs on small permissions and every one of them is revocable. The film watches maintenance, and who performs it, and what the performing costs the one who is never asked. Kinema Junpo named it the year's best and has kept it on the all-time list of Japanese films.

The defeat in this film was two years old when it was shot. The Anjo family have lost the peerage that organized their lives and the money that furnished it, the mansion is going to a creditor, and before it goes there will be one more ball, with the correct clothes, the correct music, and nobody in the room willing to say the plain thing aloud. Kōzaburō Yoshimura holds it to 89 minutes and largely to one address, which turns an evening into a pressure system: no one can leave and everyone keeps meeting. Kinema Junpo named it the best film of 1947. What gives the manners their charge is proximity, since in 1947 the collapse was not a subject but a condition, shared by the audience sitting in front of it.

Nothing in the setup is unusual: a son, a family business, parents who help run it, a girlfriend they would rather he stopped seeing. Jun takes all of it as pressure, and the pressure has nowhere to vent, because the people applying it are also the people who love him and would say so if asked. Kazuhiko Hasegawa lets the film run 121 minutes, which is long for the material and right for it, since what he is filming is a temperature rather than an event, and temperatures take time to be felt. Where this is heading is not hard to anticipate. The interest is in the domestic arithmetic that makes such a direction available at all: permission, money, meals, and affection issued in instalments against work done.

An injunction bars the striking miners from the picket line, so their wives take it instead, and the strike survives on terms nobody at the union hall would have chosen. The dispute is at the Empire Zinc mine in New Mexico, over the safety conditions and the wages the Anglo workers already have, and Ramon Quintero organizes it while treating his pregnant wife, Esperanza, roughly as the company treats him. That doubling is the film's real subject: the argument at the mine gate and the argument in the kitchen run on the same terms, and neither is settled by winning the other. An American picture of 1954 keeping both in view was not the usual practice. The National Film Registry keeps it, a Crystal Globe went to it, and it still turns up in scholarship on how Mexican labor was pictured in the United States.

Seventy-six minutes, short even by the standards of 1943, and almost none of it is spent riding. A posse takes three men it believes guilty of murder and cattle theft, and then the film stops to have the argument: hand them to a court that is distant and slow, or finish the matter here, where everyone is already assembled and already certain. The National Board of Review named it the best film of its year, and the National Film Registry keeps it. The western's usual furniture is available and largely unused; the running time goes to men talking one another toward a decision while the accused sit and listen. The pressure is procedural, which is an odd thing to say about a western and exactly what the hour is made of.

A Tiger Award went to it, which is worth knowing before the opening reels, because they do not court goodwill. Jasna is a teenager in Serbia after the wars, and her days are drink, drugs, parties and sex pursued with the persistence of a routine rather than the energy of a rebellion. Love and tenderness do enter the story eventually; the interest is in how narrow the channel for either has become, and how much of the ordinary teenage vocabulary has been replaced by exposure. Maja Miloš stays with that for 100 minutes at close range and declines to hand down a verdict on any of it. Provocation rather than sociology, then, and a film whose defenders and detractors tend to be describing the very same scenes.

Sang-hoon collects debts by hand, and the work suits him because violence is the only fluent language he was ever taught. Then a schoolgirl named Yoon-hee declines to be frightened of him and swears back, and the two fall into a friendship that neither has the equipment to conduct and neither can explain to anyone else. A Tiger Award followed. Yang Ik-june takes 130 minutes over it, and the length is the argument: nothing here is repaired by a single act of kindness, and a pattern takes about as long to loosen as it took to install. Anger in this film behaves like inherited property, passed down, collected on, paid forward with interest, and how the transfer works holds its attention far more than who is at fault.

The reason a seventeen-year-old has to leave her school is withheld, and the withholding is the design rather than a trick. Gong-ju is placed in the house of a stranger, her former teacher's mother, because her own parents are not a resource, and she starts the ordinary work of being the new girl somewhere that knows nothing about her: a room, a routine, the courtesy of people who have no idea what they are being courteous about. Lee Su-jin lets that ordinariness run for a long stretch of the 112 minutes, so the present tense builds its own weight before the past arrives to claim it. A Tiger Award went to it. The subject is custody: who takes a child in, on whose authority, and how fast generosity turns conditional once it costs something.

A muezzin's work is to be heard and not looked at, five times a day, by everyone within range. Musa does that work; his neighbor Clara is a Catholic nurse, and he falls for her with a completeness his position supplies no procedure for. Mahmut Fazıl Coşkun declines the obvious framing, since this is not an argument between a mosque and a church, and 90 minutes leaves no room for a thesis anyway. What the film spends itself on is the practical embarrassment of a man whose feeling has no permitted form, and on Yakup, a third figure whose connection to Clara rearranges the geometry without raising the volume. A Tiger Award went to it. The register stays low enough that anyone waiting for a confrontation will end up noticing other things.
